title: Bystanders and Upstanders
keyIdea: When someone is being unkind, every child who sees it makes a choice. Joining in means laughing, cheering or filming. A bystander watches and does nothing. An upstander helps in a safe way: says stop, stands with the hurt child, tells a grown-up or checks in later. If someone could get hurt, get a grown-up fast. Telling to keep someone safe is never telling tales.

kid: Zak is mean to Mia. Other kids see it. Each one has a choice. A kid who joins in laughs or cheers. A bystander just looks on. An upstander helps Mia.
Doing nothing is a choice too. If kids laugh, Zak has a crowd. If no one laughs, his show is over. So do not laugh. Walk off with Mia.
Lots of kids may see it. Each one thinks: someone else will help. Then no one does. Be the first one. Then the rest will join you.
Help in a safe way. Say: Stop, that is not kind. Ask Mia to play. If a kid could get hurt, get a grown-up fast. To tell to keep a kid safe is not to tell tales.
adult: This topic covers the bystander role in relationships education. In England, the statutory guidance for primary schools says pupils should learn about the responsibilities of bystanders, mainly reporting bullying to an adult, and how to get help. The IB PYP personal, social and physical education strand asks children to show care and stand up for others. At 7 to 9 the aim is to name the roles, choose a safe action and feel able to use it.

Key terms: a passive bystander watches and does nothing. Children who laugh, cheer or film are joining in, because they give the unkind child an audience. An upstander speaks up, stands with the target, tells an adult or checks in later. In Canadian playground studies, peers were there in most bullying episodes. When one peer stepped in, the bullying often stopped within seconds. The bystander effect, or diffusion of responsibility, is why a big crowd can mean less help: each person waits for someone else.

Common mistakes: thinking that doing nothing is neutral; thinking that laughing along is harmless; teaching children to step in with their hands, or to be mean back, which puts them at risk; and calling reporting telling tales. Be careful with the rule. Telling to keep someone safe is always right. Telling tales is telling to get someone into trouble. Safety comes first, so when someone could get hurt, the job is to fetch an adult fast.

In the lab your child sorts what each child does, stops a laughing crowd and watches the audience bar fall, and goes first so the others follow. Then they pick a safe move for scenes of low and high risk, and sort telling from telling tales.

familyTip: Agree a family upstander plan: three safe moves your child can use, such as 'Stop, that's not kind', 'Come and play with us' and telling an adult. Act them out with toys, then ask after school: did anyone need an upstander today?

visual.caption: Who is an upstander? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Says: Stop, that is not kind
Asks the hurt child to play

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort what each child does, stop a laughing crowd, be the first helper, pick a safe move for the risk, and sort telling from telling tales.

practice.prompt: Bystanders and upstanders: Kai sees Zak take Mia's ball. Kai says, 'Give it back, that is not kind.' What is Kai?
practice.hint: Did Kai help Mia, watch, or join in with Zak?
practice.explain: Kai spoke up to help Mia in a safe way, so Kai is an upstander.

practice.prompt: {n} children watch Zak tease Mia, and they all laugh. Then {k} of them stop laughing and walk off with Mia. How many are still laughing?
practice.hint: Take the children who stopped away from all the children who laughed.
practice.explain: {n} take away {k} is {=n-k}. Each child who stops laughing makes Zak's audience smaller.

practice.prompt: Two children are pushing hard and someone could get hurt. What should an upstander do?
practice.hint: When someone could get hurt, what keeps everyone safe?
practice.explain: Pushing back could get you hurt, and watching lets it go on. Get a grown-up fast.

practice.prompt: Ada is the first to help a child who is left out. Then {k} more children join her. How many helpers are there now?
practice.hint: Count Ada, then count on the children who joined her.
practice.explain: Ada plus {k} more makes {=k+1} helpers. Once one child goes first, others follow.

pool.prompt: Ivy films Zak being mean to Mia and shows her friends. What is Ivy doing?
pool.hint: Does filming help Mia, or give Zak an audience?
pool.explain: Filming and sharing it gives Zak an audience and hurts Mia more. That is joining in.

pool.prompt: Which of these is a safe upstander move?
choices: Ask the child to come and play with you
pool.hint: A safe move helps the hurt child without making it bigger.
pool.explain: Standing with the child helps them and keeps you safe. Being mean back or hitting makes it worse.

pool.prompt: Why can a big crowd mean that nobody helps?
choices: Each one waits for someone else
Nobody in a crowd can see
pool.hint: Think about what each child in the crowd is thinking.
pool.explain: Each one thinks someone else will help, so nobody does. Be the first, and others will join.

pool.prompt: {n} children watch someone being teased. {k} of them laugh. How many are only watching, not laughing?
pool.hint: Take the laughing children away from all the children watching.
pool.explain: {n} take away {k} is {=n-k} bystanders. They could still choose to help.

pool.prompt: Mia looked sad at lunch, but it is over now. What can an upstander do later?
choices: Ask Mia if she is OK
pool.hint: How can you show Mia that someone cares?
pool.explain: Checking in later is an upstander move. It shows Mia she is not on her own.

pool.prompt: You tell a teacher that a child is bullied every day. This is…
pool.hint: Telling tales is to get someone into trouble. Why are you telling?
pool.explain: You are telling to keep a child safe, so it is the right thing to do, not telling tales.

pool.prompt: Raj sees Zak being unkind and walks past without a word. What is Raj?
pool.hint: Did Raj help, join in, or do nothing?
pool.explain: Raj saw it and did nothing, so Raj is a bystander. He could choose a safe way to help.

pool.prompt: Kai stands with Mia. Then {k} friends come and stand with them. How many children stand with Mia now, not counting Mia?
pool.hint: Count Kai, then add the friends who came.
pool.explain: Kai plus {k} friends is {=k+1} children standing with Mia. A group makes the unkind child stop.
